turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Hey, come on in. I'm Dr. Ellison. Morning ran long, so thanks for waiting.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): It's fine. That TV out there is so loud I can't hear myself think. I'm, uh, pretty jumpy today, sorry.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): You're alright. What brought you in?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): It burns when I pee. That's why I came. And I'm going constantly, like every hour, even when there's barely a trickle.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): How long has the burning and all that running to the bathroom been going on?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Four days. It just showed up and it hasn't let go.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): Anything else riding along with it?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): My lower back aches, same four days. I keep thinking I've overdone it pulling orders at the warehouse, but sitting down isn't helping.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): So the warehouse is your job. What are you most worried this is?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): My kidney. Are you going to admit me? I can't miss a shift, rent's due, and I googled way too much last night.

[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm not admitting you off this story. Burning and peeing all the time for four days, plus a backache, makes me think urine infection before kidney. Tell me the rest and then I'll look at you.
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): I felt warm last night, a little fever, not drenching the sheets. And I feel like a wet rag, just wiped out. Is a little fever already an emergency?
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): A small fever can come with a bladder infection, and no, it isn't an automatic ER trip. Any discharge, any fluid coming from the penis?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Definitely not. I checked because I was scared this was an STD. Be straight with me, is it?
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): No discharge makes an STD a lot less likely, though I won't swear to it without a test. Any cough, or trouble getting your breath?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Lungs feel normal. Could this move into my chest if we wait?
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): That would be a strange path, I don't see it. Have you lost any weight?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose. Sometimes, not really. Pants still fit, so, umm, I don't actually know.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Then I won't put weight loss in as a yes or a no. How about the bowels, any diarrhea?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Bowels are normal. My buddy got home from Mexico with the runs and I panicked, but that was him.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): Did you travel yourself, anywhere recent?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I haven't gone anywhere. Sorry, frog in my throat, that's just nerves, my throat isn't sore.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll ignore the throat then. Pop this under your tongue. 99.4. That's mild, not a big fever.
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Okay, 99.4. What if it climbs at 2 a.m.? Do I call you or just go in? I need the actual rule.

[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll give you the rule after I examine you, so it fits what I find. Belly's a little tender right over the pubic bone. I tap both flanks and you don't flinch, so nothing there is jumping out as an angry kidney.
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): The ache sits low, across the middle, and it's not a sharp stab. So the kidney's okay? You're sure?
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): Less likely it's the kidney. Sure would be overselling a two-minute exam. What medicines are you on?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Ibuprofen, 400 milligrams, twice a day, these past four days, for the back. And lisinopril, 10 milligrams, every morning.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): Lisinopril for blood pressure? How long have you had that?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah. A couple of years. They tell me it's controlled. Should I stop it? Is that what's burning me?
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): Don't stop the lisinopril. Burning urine isn't how that pill usually misbehaves. Any medicine allergies?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No allergies at all. I just hate when pills make me sick. So what are you putting me on?

[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): Walking through it, mild fever, burning, frequency, a quiet flank exam, blood pressure in the background. I was going to send urine today and start nitrofurantoin, 100 milligrams by mouth, twice a day, for five days, before you left.

[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Nitrofurantin? No, please. I took that last year for the same kind of burning and I threw up the whole next day, so I stopped after two doses. Will every antibiotic do that, and does my wife need a test too?
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): That changes it. Scratch the nitrofurantoin, I'm not handing you a medicine that made you vomit, and I'm not starting any antibiotic before the urine result.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): So I walk out with nothing? How long until you know? What if I get worse tonight while we're waiting?

[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll do a urinalysis and a urine culture before you leave today. If the test shows an infection, I'll call in an antibiotic that isn't nitrofurantoin. And if you're not better in three days, come back and see me.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): If I start shaking or puking, I shouldn't wait for that call, right? And can I work my shift tomorrow or am I done?

[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right. Shaking chills, vomiting, or you can't keep fluids down, go to the ER, don't wait on me. Drink water through the day, keep the ibuprofen if your stomach allows, and work is fine if a bathroom's close.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): I keep thinking it's cancer, err, or my prostate, because some forum said so. I need you to say what you actually think.

[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): My working read is a lower urinary tract infection. I can't fully rule out some early prostate irritation, but nothing here screams cancer, and I want the urine back before I talk like it's settled.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm 46, does that make the prostate thing more likely? Also, um, sex. Should we hold off? I hate asking.
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): 46 doesn't change the plan. Hold off on sex until the burning eases. Your wife doesn't need testing based on this visit.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): Okay. Cup today, no script in my hand, you call only if I need a different antibiotic. Am I missing a piece?
[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): That's the whole of it. Lab's down the hall on the left, they'll take the sample on your way out.
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): Alright. I walked in sure you were keeping me overnight. One last thing, is coffee gonna make the burn worse?
[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): Coffee can poke at an irritated bladder, so skip it for a couple of days if you can stand to. Water's the better move.
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): Okay. Water, then the cup. Thanks for not rushing me out confused.

spec.situation: Man with burning urine, frequency and lower back ache for four days; fever mild; denies discharge; no recent travel; urine test and antibiotic planned, conditional on result.

traps.happens: The patient describes things in colourful or sentence-like speech ('I've overdone it', 'I can't hear myself think', 'a frog in my throat', 'my feet feel dead', 'I feel like a wet rag').
traps.label_rule: Every symptom name is a short clinical noun phrase of 1 to 5 words ('voice fatigue', 'numbness in both feet', 'tiredness'), never a full sentence, never starting with I/we/my. Pure idioms that are not symptoms ('I can't hear myself think' said about classroom noise) are NOT symptoms. The patient's own words stay in the cited turn, not in the name.

traps.happens: The doctor asks only two to four review-of-systems questions (for example fever, weight, cough). Several other body systems are never asked about. One of the asked questions gets a vague or mixed answer.
traps.label_rule: negative_findings / review_of_systems ONLY for items the doctor actually asked AND the patient answered, evidence = that question and answer. Never add review-of-systems entries for systems nobody asked about, and never cite an unrelated turn (for example a turn about tiredness) for a system review.

features: ambiguous_answer: an answer that sounds like yes but is really 'maybe' ('mm, I suppose', 'sometimes, not really'); recorded with uncertainty or not at all, never as a firm fact.
doctor_changes_mind: the doctor says one plan, then changes it after new information; the label holds the final plan.

bad.reason: Past nitrofurantoin use and stopping after two doses are supported; indication was same burning last year, not current discontinued medication.

omissions.text: Patient has no weight-loss history established; clinician explicitly stated weight loss would not be recorded as yes or no because the patient was unsure.
Patient denied sore throat ('my throat isn't sore').
Back pain was characterized as low/across the middle and not sharp/stabbing.
Nitrofurantoin was initially planned at 100 mg by mouth twice a day for 5 days before being canceled.
Patient previously took nitrofurantoin last year for similar urinary burning, vomited the whole next day, and stopped after two doses; this was intolerance/adverse effect rather than a true allergy.
Doctor advised not to stop lisinopril.
Doctor said wife does not need testing based on this visit.
Doctor said nothing here screams cancer.

omissions.text: Urinary output detail: patient said he is going constantly 'every hour' even when there is 'barely a trickle' (small-volume voids).
Weight loss was specifically queried but left indeterminate: patient said he did not actually know, and doctor stated he would not record weight loss as yes or no.

History related to nitrofurantoin is recorded incorrectly as a medication rather than an intolerance/adverse reaction: patient said last year nitrofurantoin for similar urinary burning caused him to 'throw up the whole next day' and he stopped after two doses; doctor therefore cancelled nitrofurantoin.
Doctor's provisional assessment explicitly included that the presentation was 'urine infection before kidney' and that the exam did not suggest 'an angry kidney' / kidney involvement was less likely.
